meta.title: Who really said "Never express yourself more clearly than you are able to think"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Bohr's colleagues reported his precept never to speak more clearly than one thinks; the popular 'express yourself' wording has no primary source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never express yourself more clearly than you are able to think'?
meta.ogDescription: The idea is Niels Bohr's, reported by Abraham Pais in 1967, but the popular 'express yourself' wording comes from quotation books, not from Bohr.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The idea is well documented as Bohr’s own: Abraham Pais, who worked with him, wrote in 1967 of “Bohr’s precept never to speak more clearly than one thinks,” and other writers quote him in the first person (“I try not to speak more clearly than I think”). But no primary source contains this exact “express yourself” wording. It is a later quotation-book version of the saying.

source.heading: The closest documented source

docMeta.dd: Abraham Pais, “Reminiscences from the Postwar Years”
Niels Bohr: His Life and Work as Seen by His Friends and Colleagues
Stefan Rozental, ed. · North-Holland, Amsterdam, 1967; reprinted in Niels Bohr: A Centenary Volume (Harvard University Press, 1985)

source.excerpt: Bohr was divinely bad as a public speaker. This was not due to his precept never to speak more clearly than one thinks. Had he done so, the outcome would have been quite different, as Bohr was a man of the greatest lucidity of thought.
trail: Wikiquote lists the popular wording among Bohr’s quotes, but its only citation is a 2004 compilation, Jason Merchey’s Values of the Wise, p. 63 (Wikiquote ↗). Quote Investigator has no entry for this quote.
Abraham Pais’s 1967 reminiscence in Stefan Rozental’s volume describes “Bohr’s precept never to speak more clearly than one thinks” (Open Library full-text search ↗).
First-person versions are quoted by Lincoln Barnett (1964), Ruth Moore (1966) and Richard Rhodes, all with “speak more clearly than I think” (Open Library full-text search ↗).
The “express yourself … are able to think” wording shows up in quotation books, not in writing by Bohr or people who knew him (Open Library full-text search ↗).
source.excerptNote: Text as reprinted in Niels Bohr: A Centenary Volume (1985). The 1967 original reads “Bohr’s precept.” This is Pais describing Bohr’s saying, not the popular wording.

sourceLink.text: Pais’s passage in scanned editions (Open Library full-text search)

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording has no identifiable source, so we make no copyright claim for it. The documented versions appear in works first published from 1964 onward (Barnett 1964, Moore 1966, Pais 1967, Rhodes 1986). All of those are after 1931, so they are presumably still in copyright.

author.name: Niels Bohr
author.heading: About Niels Bohr
author.metaLine: 1885–1962 · Danish physicist, Nobel Prize in Physics 1922
author.bio: Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist whose quantum model of the atom earned him the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics. He led the Copenhagen institute that became a center of early quantum mechanics. Colleagues remembered him for his careful thinking and his halting, hard-to-follow way of speaking. He had a saying about not speaking more clearly than one thinks.

misattribution.heading: How the wording drifted
misattribution.intro: Bohr’s saying was passed along in many forms. The imperative version on posters and quote sites is the most polished one, and the least sourced. The same line has also been credited to other people.

items.who: “Never express yourself more clearly than you are able to think”
items.why: Every source written by someone close to Bohr has “speak more clearly than I/one think(s).” The “express yourself … are able to think” form shows up in quotation books such as a 1997 scan of The Ultimate Book of Business Quotations (which spells his name “Niels Bohrs”) (Open Library ↗). A shorter version, “Never express yourself more clearly than you think,” appears in an entry of Jay Scott’s satirical Daily Whale dated 20 January 1992 (posted in his online archive) (the Daily Whale ↗).

items.who: “Never express yourself more clearly than you can think”
items.why: A 1999 physics mailing-list post quotes this version and says it “has been attributed to Niels Bohr” (phys-l archive ↗).
Marvin Minsky’s The Society of Mind (1986) opens its postscript with “Never speak more clearly than you think. — Jeremy Bernstein,” and later books repeat that credit (Open Library ↗).

Simpson’s Contemporary Quotations credits “Never speak more clearly than you think” to Baker on becoming President Reagan’s chief of staff, and David Crystal’s Words on Words also credits Baker (Open Library ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Bohr’s. Abraham Pais, who worked with him, called it “Bohr’s precept never to speak more clearly than one thinks” in 1967 (Open Library ↗). The tidy “express yourself” wording is a later quotation-book version.

context.heading: Why Bohr said it
lead: Bohr was famous for speaking slowly and haltingly, often with qualifications. His colleague Abraham Pais remembered him as “divinely bad as a public speaker.” Pais insisted this was not because of “his precept never to speak more clearly than one thinks,” since Bohr’s thinking was very clear (Open Library full-text search ↗).

The saying shows up in many first-person forms from people writing about Bohr. Lincoln Barnett (1964) has “I must never speak more clearly than I think.” Ruth Moore (1966) has “You see the problem is never to speak more clearly than I think.” Richard Rhodes (1986) has “I try not to speak more clearly than I think” (Open Library full-text search ↗). So many variants suggest a real habit of speech with no single fixed wording.
detailsBody: In The Making of the Atomic Bomb (Simon & Schuster, 1986), Rhodes’s endnote credits “I try not to speak more clearly than I think” to J. Robert Oppenheimer’s 1963 lectures “Niels Bohr and His Times.” Rhodes’s bibliography lists those lectures as unpublished manuscripts in the Oppenheimer Papers. That makes it secondhand testimony, not something Bohr wrote.
context.pull: Bohr was divinely bad as a public speaker. This was not due to his precept never to speak more clearly than one thinks.
